questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presented with a painful, red, purulent port site and fevers. He had pancreatic cancer and an implanted port for chemotherapy. On exam, the port site was erythematous, with a central area of fluctuance, and some visible purulence. His temperature was 37.2°C, heart rate 98 beats/minute, and blood pressure 108/64 mmHg. Investigations: Neutrophil count 7.2 ×109/L Alkaline phosphatase 95 U/L Empiric antibiotic therapy was started while plans were made for his port to be removed.
questions.lead_in: What antibiotic is an essential component of empirical treatment?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin Central-line associated infections are most commonly caused by gram-positive organisms, most notably Staphylococcus and Streptococcus spp. MRSA is sufficiently prevalent to warrant empiric coverage with vancomycin or another effective agent, and parenteral therapy should be considered until bacteremia is excluded.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q15

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man with ESRD on hemodialysis and difficult intravenous access needed new intravenous access to be placed for daily administration of parenteral medications.
questions.lead_in: What type of intravenous catheter carries the highest risk of bloodstream infection?
questions.explanation: Nontunneled femoral CVC Risk of bloodstream infection from IV access varies based on type of catheter and site of placement. Non-tunneled CVCs (central venous catheters) have higher rates of infections than tunneled catheters, PICCs (peripherally inserted central catheters), and peripheral IVs. Femoral placement confers a higher risk of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) than internal jugular and subclavian insertions. Type of catheter: Peripheral IV < PICC < Tunneled central venous catheter (CVC) < Nontunneled CVC Site of CVC: Subclavian < Internal jugular < Femoral CVC
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q15

questions.stem: Catheter-retention in the setting of central lineassociated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is sometimes attempted depending on disease severity, alternative IV access options, and pathogenicity of the organism identified.
questions.lead_in: According to recommendations, long-term catheter retention may be attempted if blood cultures are positive for what organisms?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis IDSA guidelines suggest that long-term CVCs should be removed in the circumstance of a CLABSI from all of the organisms listed, apart from S. epidermidis . Catheter removal, however, in this circumstance can shorten the needed antibiotic duration and can reduce the risk of relapsed BSI from any residual biofilm formation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q16

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fevers, malaise, and redness around the site of a longterm indwelling IV line in place for cancer chemotherapy. She had a history of metastatic cervical cancer. She had no known drug allergies. On physical exam, some purulence was expressed from the IV line site. Investigations: Total white cell count 12.5 ×109/L Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL Platelets 55 ×109/L Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Gram-stain of exit site pus showed GPC in clusters Blood cultures obtained through both the longterm indwelling IV line, as well from a peripheral vein, were positive for Staphylococcus aureus, with susceptibilities pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial empiric treatment of this patient’s bacteremia?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) must be covered empirically, pending sensitivities. Dalbavancin is not established for treatment of infections other than acute bacterial skin/skin structure infections. Linezolid should be avoided for treatment of line-related bacteremias due to inferior efficacy in that setting. Clindamycin is not as reliably active against MRSA as vancomycin and is not established as a preferred treatment for MRSA bloodstream infection. There are no apparent contraindications or concerns with using vancomycin in this case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q4

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman was reviewed in the intensive care with fever and hemodynamic instability. She was recently repatriated to a rehabilitation hospital in the United States from India, where she had been hospitalized for 3 months because of a cerebrovascular accident. She had a peripherally inserted central catheter for blood work, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube for supplemental alimentation, and an indwelling urinary catheter. Five days earlier, she had developed fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. She was started on meropenem and fluconazole. Investigations: PICC and peripheral blood cultures: positive for Candida haemulonii after 72 hours; susceptibility as follows: Agent Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) or Mean Effective Concentration (MEC) Interpretation Fluconazole 128 μg/mL Resistant Amphotericin B 2 μg/mL Resistant Micafungin 0.5 μg/mL Susceptible
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely correct identification of the organism?
questions.explanation: Candida auris Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen that causes otomycosis and invasive candidiasis. It is an important nosocomial pathogen, especially in some parts of the world where it has already established endemicity. Healthcareassociated outbreaks have been reported in the United States. C. auris will be misidentified by commercial identification systems. The Vitek-2 will usually misidentify C. auris as Candida haemulonii and sometimes as Candida famata; the API-20C system will misidentify C. auris as Rhodotorula glutinis, Candida sake, or Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The correct identification can be made through DNA sequencing or with matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q25

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man was reviewed with a 4-day history of fevers and hypotension despite empiric use of broadspectrum antibiotics. The man had presented to hospital 3 weeks earlier with profuse diarrhea and severe malnutrition. He had Crohn’s disease with short gut syndrome secondary to multiple bowel resections. He was initiated at admission on total parenteral nutrition via central venous catheter. His antimicrobials were changed to meropenem and micafungin. Investigations: Total white cell count 20 ×109/L Platelet count 50 ×109/L Blood cultures (central and peripheral) no growth after 3 days CXR: bilateral airspace disease
questions.lead_in: What is the best next test to secure a diagnosis?

options.text: Blood culture inoculated onto Sabouraud dextrose agar
Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil

questions.explanation: Blood culture on Sabouraud dextrose with olive oil This is a case of disseminated Malassezia infection. Risk factors in this case include CVC and lipid infusions (TPN). Malassezia spp. are intrinsically resistant to echinocandins, thus a response to micafungin is not expected. Malassezia spp. are lipophilic, and all species but M. pachydermatis require exogenous lipids for growth. M. furfur is the most common pathogen involved in disseminated disease. Recovery from standard blood cultures is low unless the media is enriched with fatty acids, i.e., with olive oil, palmitic acid, Tween, etc., or with Dixon’s agar, which contains glycerol mono-oleate. Serum 1,3- β-D-glucan is a nonspecific biomarker of fungal disease. It is not particularly helpful in making a diagnosis. Panfungal PCR is not useful on blood because of the low burden of organisms in the total circulation. Serum CrAg is used for the diagnosis of cryptococcosis (including subclinical disease). It also can cross react with Trichosporon spp. in disseminated disease, although a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. Trichosporonosis has been reported in neonates but is less likely than Malassezia disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q26

questions.question: Central venous catheter (CVC)-associated infections.

parts.text: If there are 4 confirmed CVC-BSI in 200 patients, 800 days and 250 catheter days, what is the rate of infection using the most appropriate units?
What are five interventions to decrease CVC-BSI rates?
Name 3 routes of acquisition of bloodstream infection in CVCs (there are actually 4 routes).

parts_raw.text: If 4 confirmed CVC-BSI in 200 patients, 800 days and 250 catheter days, what is the rate of infections using the most appropriate units.
b) What are five interventions to decrease CVC-BSI rates?
c) Name 3 routes of acquisition of BSI in CVCs. (There are actually 4 routes)

questions.model_answer:
a) The appropriate denominator is catheter-days, expressed per 1000 catheter-days: (4 CVC-BSI / 250 catheter-days) x 1000 = 16 CVC-BSI per 1000 catheter-days.
b) (1) Educate/train all personnel involved in insertion and maintenance. (2) Hand hygiene before insertion and manipulation. (3) Maximal sterile barrier precautions at insertion (mask, cap, sterile gown/gloves, large sterile drape). (4) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine in alcohol, allowed to dry; avoid the femoral site. (5) Daily assessment of ongoing need and prompt removal of nonessential catheters, plus disinfection of hubs/injection ports with friction for >=5 seconds before access.
c) (1) Contamination of the infusate. (2) Contamination of the catheter hub/lumen (intraluminal source). (3) Contamination of skin at the insertion site with extraluminal migration (extraluminal source). [4th route: hematogenous seeding of the catheter from a distant focus of infection.]

cohort_answer.text:
# infections/cath days x1000 = (4/250) x 1000 = 16 per 1000 days; # infections/#days in that month x 1000 = (4/800) x 1000
Designate only trained personnel who demonstrate competence for the insertion and maintenance of CVCs; Use maximum sterile barrier precautions when inserting CVC; Hand hygiene before and after manipulating the CVC; Educate HCW regarding indications, maintenance and infection control measures to prevent CVC infections; Do not use topical abx ointment/creams on insertion site may promote AMR/fungal infx. Exception is dialysis cath.; Remove when no longer indicated; Prep with chlorohexidine 0.5%; Avoid femoral cathethers
Cath colonization with biofilm; During manipulation; Skin colonization; Haematogenic spread; During infusion from contaminated IV products

questions.question: A patient 10 days after insertion of a prosthetic knee develops fever for 24 hours. She has a well-functioning PICC line with no erythema or discharge at the site, and the surgeon orders it removed. Follow-up urine and blood cultures are negative; the catheter tip culture is positive for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). You are consulted for management of a "line-related infection".
questions.question_raw: A patient 10 days post op after insertion of a prosthetic knee. She develops a fever post for 24 hours. She has a PICC line in place and the surgeon orders the line to be removed. Prior to removal, the line is functioning well with no erythema or discharge around the site. Follow-up cultures are negative in the urine and blood. Tip culture is positive for MSSA. You are consulted for management of a "line-related infection".

parts.text: What 2 things would you advise the surgeon?

parts_raw.text: What 2 things would you advise the surgeon

questions.model_answer: a) (1) This is catheter tip colonization, not a CLABSI: there is no local site infection and blood cultures are negative, so there is no evidence of systemic catheter-related infection and removal of the already-removed line is sufficient management of the line itself. (2) Do not attribute the fever to the line - actively evaluate the prosthetic knee (and other sources) as the cause of the postoperative fever, and, because the organism is S. aureus, draw surveillance/repeat blood cultures and monitor closely for occult bacteremia.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA catheter-related infection guideline (Mermel 2009): for a positive S. aureus tip culture with negative blood cultures, obtain surveillance blood cultures and consider a short (5-7 day) course of antistaphylococcal therapy given the risk of endocarditis; Mandell text (pp. 3570-3571) supports removal for S. aureus but does not address the negative-culture tip-colonization scenario.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort says no antibiotics are needed; current IDSA guidance for an S. aureus-positive tip advises surveillance blood cultures and considering a brief antistaphylococcal course because of endocarditis risk.

cohort_answer.text: No evidence of systemic infection, removal of line is sufficient, no systemic abx needed. Evaluate knee as source of infection.

questions.question: CLABSI surveillance. February: 15 positive isolates, 150 patients, 1500 patient-days, 1000 central line-days. March: 10 positive isolates, 150 patients, 2000 patient-days, 1000 central line-days.
questions.question_raw: CLABSI question. February: 15 positive isolates, 150 patients, 1500 patient days, 1000 central line days. March: 10 positive isolates, 150 patients, 2000 patient days, 1000 central line days.

parts.text: What was the rate of CLABSI in February (in standard units, per 100,000 central line-days)?
What is the catheter utilization ratio?
You find out that ALL of the CLABSI isolates are MRSA. What is the attack rate?

parts_raw.text: What was the rate of CLABSI in February (in standard units, per 100,000 central line days)
What is the catheter utilization ratio?
You find out that ALL of the CLABSI isolates are MRSA. What is the attack rate?

questions.model_answer:
a) CLABSI rate = (CLABSI / central line-days) x 100,000 = (15 / 1000) x 100,000 = 1500 CLABSI per 100,000 central line-days (equivalent to 15 per 1000 central line-days).
b) Catheter utilization ratio = central line-days / patient-days. February alone = 1000/1500 = 0.67; over the two months combined = (1000+1000)/(1500+2000) = 2000/3500 = 0.57.
c) Attack rate = new cases / persons at risk = (15+10) / (150+150) = 25/300 = 0.083 = 8.3%.
questions.beyond_mandell: Definitions per CDC/NHSN surveillance methodology (CLABSI rate per 1000 or 100,000 central line-days; catheter utilization ratio = central line-days/patient-days); not derived from the Mandell chapter text.

cohort_answer.text: Rate Feb: 15/1000 x 100000 = 1500 per 100,000 central line days (or 15 per 1000 central line days). Catheter utilization ratio (CUR) = catheter days/patient days = 2000/3500 = 0.57. Attack rate = new cases/persons at risk = 25/300 = 0.083 (8.3%)

questions.question: Central line infections in a dialysis unit.
questions.question_raw: Central line infections in dialysis unit

parts.text: What is the central line with the lowest rate of CL-BSI recommended for use in dialysis patients?
Name 6 core IPAC measures to reduce BSI in a dialysis unit.

parts_raw.text: What is the central line with the lowest rate of CL BSI recommended for use in dialysis patients
Name 6 core IPAC measures to reduce BSI in a dialysis unit

questions.model_answer:
a) The recommended vascular access with the lowest infection risk is a native arteriovenous (AV) fistula; when a catheter is unavoidable, a tunneled cuffed catheter placed in the internal jugular vein carries the lowest catheter-related BSI risk (femoral and subclavian sites are avoided).
b) (1) Hand hygiene before and after every access/manipulation. (2) Aseptic technique with maximal sterile barriers for catheter insertion. (3) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine-alcohol, allowed to dry. (4) Disinfect catheter hubs/ports with mechanical friction for >=5 seconds before each access. (5) Daily assessment of catheter need with prompt removal of unnecessary catheters (and preferential use of AV fistula/graft over catheters). (6) Staff education/competency, BSI surveillance with feedback, and antimicrobial (e.g., mupirocin or povidone-iodine) ointment at the catheter exit site in patients with recurrent S. aureus infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Dialysis BSI Prevention Collaborative core interventions and KDOQI vascular-access guidance (AV fistula as preferred lowest-risk access; surveillance/feedback; catheter exit-site antimicrobial ointment) are not developed in the Mandell chapter, which covers the general prevention bundle.

questions.model_answer:
a) A native arteriovenous (AV) fistula is the vascular access with the lowest infectious risk (risk increases through AV graft, then tunneled cuffed catheter, then non-tunneled catheter).
b) (1) Hand hygiene before and after every access. (2) Aseptic/maximal-barrier technique for catheter insertion and care. (3) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine-alcohol, allowed to dry. (4) Disinfect catheter hubs/connectors with friction for >=5 seconds before each access. (5) Minimize catheter use and days - daily assessment of need, promote conversion to AV fistula/graft. (6) Staff and patient education, routine BSI surveillance with feedback, and antimicrobial ointment at the catheter exit site for recurrent S. aureus infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: AV fistula as the lowest-risk access and dialysis-specific core interventions (surveillance/feedback, exit-site antimicrobial ointment) rest on CDC dialysis BSI prevention and KDOQI guidance, not the Mandell chapter itself.

questions.model_answer:
a) A native arteriovenous (AV) fistula is the least risky vascular access and the recommended approach.
b) (1) Hand hygiene before and after every access. (2) Aseptic technique with maximal sterile barriers at insertion. (3) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine-alcohol, allowed to dry. (4) Disinfect catheter hubs/ports with mechanical friction for >=5 seconds before each access. (5) Daily assessment of catheter need with prompt removal, minimizing catheter use in favour of AV fistula/graft. questions.beyond_mandell: AV fistula as lowest-risk access and the dialysis-specific interventions (surveillance/feedback, exit-site antimicrobial ointment) derive from CDC dialysis BSI prevention and KDOQI guidance rather than the Mandell chapter.

parts_raw.text: For enterobacterales, what 3 antibiotics can be tested by disk diffusion directly on a blood culture sample according to CLSI guidelines?
What is 1 non-enterobacterales bacteria to the species level for which this method also has valid breakpoints?
List 5 essential practices from the most recent IDSA/SHEA guidelines to prevent CLABSI during line insertion

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ceftriaxone. (2) Meropenem. (3) Ciprofloxacin. (Ampicillin, ceftazidime, aztreonam, tobramycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are also validated for direct-from-positive-blood-culture disk diffusion with 16-20 h reading.)

b) Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

c) (1) Hand hygiene immediately before insertion. (2) Full maximal sterile barrier precautions - cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves and a full-body sterile drape. (3) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine in alcohol, allowed to dry. (4) Optimal site selection - subclavian preferred over internal jugular and avoid the femoral vein in adults; use ultrasound guidance to reduce attempts. (5) Insertion only by trained/competent personnel using a checklist with an empowered observer able to stop the procedure for breaches, and daily review with prompt removal of unnecessary catheters.

questions.model_answer:
a) In a hemodialysis/nephrology population the lowest-risk vascular access is a native AV fistula; when a catheter must be used, a tunneled cuffed catheter in the internal jugular vein carries the lowest risk (subclavian is avoided because of stenosis, and femoral has the highest risk).
b) (1) Hand hygiene before insertion and every manipulation. (2) Maximal sterile barrier precautions at insertion (mask, cap, sterile gown/gloves, large drape). (3) Skin antisepsis with >0.5% chlorhexidine-alcohol, allowed to dry before puncture. (4) Disinfect catheter hubs/injection ports with friction for >=5 seconds before each access. (5) Daily assessment of catheter need and prompt removal of nonessential catheters; avoid femoral placement and promote AV fistula. (6) Daily chlorhexidine bathing of ICU patients, staff education, and BSI surveillance with feedback.
questions.beyond_mandell: AV fistula as lowest-risk hemodialysis access and dialysis-specific core interventions are from CDC dialysis BSI prevention and KDOQI guidance; the Mandell chapter provides the general prevention bundle.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort states subclavian is the lowest-risk site; for hemodialysis the lowest-risk access is a native AV fistula, and the subclavian vein is specifically avoided because of stenosis that jeopardizes future access.

cohort_answer.text: Subclavian = lowest rate of infection. Recommendations: aseptic technique for insertion; handwash before insertion; sterile barriers (mask, cap, gown, sterile gloves, sterile drapes); minimize times accessed; daily chlorhexidine bathing in ICU patients >2 months of age; scrub port with friction immediately before access with appropriate antiseptic (chlorhexidine, 70% alcohol); prepare insertion site with >0.5% chlorhexidine+alcohol, must dry before insertion; daily audit to assess if line needed.

parts.text: What are your next management steps for the catheter and for antimicrobial treatment?
Name a test to differentiate albicans versus non-albicans, and indicate the expected result for Candida albicans.
The isolate is non-albicans. Do you change anything in your management, and if so, what?

The candida is identified as Candida haemulonii with high MIC to azoles, echinocandins and amphotericin. However, you do not believe this result. What do you suspect? Are there any special precautions to take?

parts_raw.text: What is your next management steps for the catheter and for antimicrobial treatment?
Name a test to differentiate albicans vs non albicans, and indicate what the expected result is for C. albicans.
The isolate is non-albicans. Do you change anything in your management, and if so, what?

The candida is identified as C. haemulonii with high MIC to azoles, echinocandins and amphotericin. However, you do not believe this result. What do you suspect? Are there any special precautions to take?

questions.model_answer:
a) Catheter: remove (or at least change) the central venous catheter — removal is almost always required for cure of catheter-associated candidemia. Antimicrobial: start empiric echinocandin (caspofungin 70 mg load then 50 mg IV daily, OR micafungin 100 mg IV daily, OR anidulafungin 200 mg load then 100 mg IV daily); also do funduscopic/ophthalmologic exam and repeat blood cultures.
b) Germ tube test — C. albicans is germ tube positive (forms true germ tubes; C. dubliniensis also positive).
c) No fundamental change — an echinocandin is the recommended first-line agent for candidemia including non-albicans species (C. glabrata, C. krusei). Continue the echinocandin; step down to fluconazole only if the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible, the patient is clinically stable and blood cultures have cleared.
d) Suspect Candida auris (frequently misidentified as C. haemulonii). Precautions: single room with contact precautions, notify infection prevention and public health/reference lab for confirmatory identification, and reinforce environmental disinfection and hand hygiene.
questions.beyond_mandell: C. auris misidentification as C. haemulonii and its infection-control measures (contact precautions, single room, public health notification) are CDC guidance, not in this chapter.
